details: CONFIRMED by experiment. On master, subprocess.run started the gate in the test runner's process group, so any signal to that
group reached relay gate. relay gate traps SIGTERM and SIGHUP (relay_gate.py:188) and its finally kills its command's own
session (line 218). The new helper passes start_new_session=True, so the gate gets a session and group of its own. A group-wide
stop of the runner no longer reaches it. Python's default SIGTERM kills the runner without running the helper's
`except BaseException`, so nothing stops the gate. The orphan seen on 26 Oct also had PPID 1, so its runner died while the gate
lived. This change makes that outcome more likely, not less.
The new test passes with the regression in place: it only exercises the case where the runner survives.
Size: 15 agent minutes. Remove start_new_session and use proc.terminate() rather than killpg, then add a regression test that
stops a runner's group and asserts no gate is left.

failing_case: A test runner (its own process group) runs Fixture.gate with a gate command that never ends (`exec sleep 120`). The runner's
process group is then sent SIGTERM. A process group gets this signal when an outer `relay gate` stops bin/ci (relay_gate.py
SIGKILLs the command's group), when a wrapper kills a job by its pgid, or when a terminal hangs up.
Now (this branch): the runner dies with rc -15. A `relay gate` process with its cwd in relay-gate-*/main/.worktrees/x is still
running, re-parented to PID 1, and so is its command. Nothing will ever stop it: the 900 s timeout lived in the dead runner.
On master the same sequence leaves no gate and no command: the gate shared the runner's group, got SIGTERM, and its handler ended
fix_hint: Drop start_new_session=True so the gate stays in the runner's group. Stop it with proc.terminate() and then proc.kill() on that
one pid, rather than os.killpg on its own group. Add a test like exp/launch.py: a child runner in its own session runs the helper,
the test stops the runner's group, and asserts that no relay gate is left with its cwd in the tmp folder.
pass_cases: 1. Runner group gets SIGTERM while Fixture.gate waits on a gate whose command sleeps: 3 s later no `relay gate` process has its cwd under the test's tmp folder, and the command's pid is gone.
2. Runner group gets SIGKILL (the outer gate's killpg) in the same setup: the gate process is gone right away (it was in the group). Its command may then outlive it, see F3.
3. test_a_gate_that_outlives_its_timeout_is_stopped_with_its_command (timeout=3, `exec sleep 600`) still passes: AssertionError "still running", and the command's pid is gone.
4. The Gate and Inert tests that end normally keep their outcomes: same return codes, the log in .relay/checks.
reason: tests/test_gate_stops.py:67 passes; it fails with the old helper (start_new_session=True): the command stays alive after SIGTERM to the runner group.

details: CONFIRMED by experiment. The comment "the gate must not be left behind either" holds for the gate, but not for what the gate
started. relay gate frees its command only on a signal it can catch. SIGKILL skips that, and killpg of the gate's own group
cannot reach the command's separate session. The timeout path does it right (terminate, then wait), and this path should do the
same.
Size: 5 agent minutes.

On master the gate got the SIGINT, raised KeyboardInterrupt, and its finally killed the command: "command alive: False".
fix_hint: In the BaseException branch, do as the timeout branch does: proc.terminate(), then communicate(timeout=GATE_STOP_GRACE), and
proc.kill() only if that times out.
pass_cases: 1. SIGINT to the runner's group during Fixture.gate with a gate command that sleeps: KeyboardInterrupt reaches the test, and 3 s later neither the gate nor its command's pid is alive.
2. A KeyboardInterrupt raised inside the helper by other means (the gate not signalled): the helper ends the gate with SIGTERM and waits, and the command's pid is gone.
